explanation: Charred crumbs from a hearth at Shubayqa in Jordan show hunter-gatherers baking flatbread from wild cereals thousands of years before wheat was domesticated.

claims.text: Charred flatbread remains found at Shubayqa 1 in north-eastern Jordan are about 14,400 years old, the oldest known direct evidence of bread.
Wheat was first domesticated less than 12,000 years ago, in south-west Asia.
The Shubayqa bread was made by hunter-gatherers from wild cereals, thousands of years before wheat was domesticated.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3). Lint: content:check run on the batch until this item showed no errors. Claims: every checkable statement is listed, distractors included; risk is at or above the C26 floor (high: c1, c2, c3). The item is counterintuitive, so its key claim (both labels, for a comparison) is high under the C26 floor; where no other reason applies, checker_doubt stands in for the guide's 'counterintuitive', which the schema's riskReason enum lacks. Datasets: No pinned dataset covers this food fact (the manifest holds countries, cities, elements, languages, currencies, Nobel prizes, World Cups, Olympic Games and artists), so the claims rest on checker knowledge, with external evidence needed for the high-risk ones. Rival test: b uses a bound, under 12,000 years ago, rather than a disputed exact date for domestication, so the answer holds under every dating I know; earlier trial cultivation of wild cereals is not domesticated wheat. Volatility: slow, because 'earliest known bread' is a record a new find could move (an older find would only widen the gap). The schema requires a reviewBy date for slow items, so I entered 1 October 2028 as a suggestion; the editor sets the final date at acceptance. Regional: nobody's school teaches this; it is equally new everywhere. Style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens, single quotation marks, explanation of 23 words. Myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches any claim. Mystery and encore checks: not applicable to a practice item. Seed: 5: nearly everyone assumes farming came first. Doubts: c1 needs a web source (the find was published in 2018 by Arranz-Otaegui and colleagues); c2 is written as a bound for that reason.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Shubayqa 1 is a Natufian hunter-gatherer site in northeastern Jordan's Black Desert. Radiocarbon dates from charred plant remains in its fireplaces fall around 14.4–14.2 thousand years ago, and the site as a whole spans roughly 14.6–11.6 thousand years ago ([2-4](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1801071115), [4-4](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10052964/)). ... The study presents this as the earliest direct evidence of bread-like preparation, about 4,000 years before agriculture emerged in southwest Asia ([2-6](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1801071115)).

claimResults.note: Attributed to the 2018 PNAS paper and its UCL Discovery copy (Tier A, the peer-reviewed study). The summary also notes a thesis giving about 14,600 years and a Wikipedia page giving 12,500 BC (about 14,450 years ago); both still fit 'about 14,400 years', so no conflict with the claim as written.
